newsitem.title: USA: Dispute delays WTO ag trade talks - USDA's Rominger.
newsitem.headline: Dispute delays WTO ag trade talks - USDA's Rominger.

text.p: World trade officials shelved agricultural issues until later this week due to a spat over how much emphasis to put on freer farm trade, Deputy U.S. Agriculture Secretary Richard Rominger said Tuesday.
Speaking to reporters by telephone from the World Trade Organization meeting in Singapore, Rominger said agriculture would not be discussed until Friday, the final day.

"They've...postponed agriculture because there is some disagreement among the agricultural countries here on exactly what the language should be in the final declaration of the conference," Rominger said. "So, we're still working."

The Cairns Group of farm exporting nations, led by Argentina, want the WTO declaration to put more emphasis on freer agricultural trade and perhaps a speedier removal of trade barriers. Others, including Japan and the European Union, favor less emphasis on the subject, Rominger said.
The U.S. delegation to the meeting included 30 representatives of the agricultural sector.
"We want to keep the emphasis on agriculture," Rominger said.

"But we also want to come out of this conference, at the end of the week, with agreement rather than acrimony because the main thing that we want to get out of it is the beginning in 1997 of preparations for the next round (of trade talks). So we don't want everybody going home here mad at each other."

The meeting, the first ministerial-level conference since WTO was formed two years ago, allowed a review of pledges to sharply reduce the use of agricultural subsidies. Rominger said some nations, like Hungary and the Philippines, have been slow to live up to commitments. He said others, such as Japan, South Korea and the EU, were reluctant to launch new reforms.
"We wanted to make sure we do stay on the time schedule and not have any delays in the next round," he said.

WTO planned a new round of trade talks in 1999. The United States wants to muzzle so-called state trading enterprises, which can operate as monopolies on exports and imports of some goods. It also wants a new agreement to further reduce tariffs and remove barriers to markets worldwide.
